I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
deliberately try to leave my body or blank out

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

vignette: As he walked onto the construction site each morning, Jason couldn't help but notice the smell of freshly cut wood and the sound of machinery humming in the distance. It was a familiar scent, one that had been imprinted on his mind since childhood, when his father would take him to visit the family's woodworking shop. But now, it was tainted by another memory - the day he witnessed the fatal crane collapse at the old site. Jason still recalled the visual memories of that day with vivid clarity: the twisted metal, the screams of his coworkers, and the eerie silence that followed. He remembered the taste of dust in his mouth and the acrid smell of smoke as he rushed to call 911. The event had left him shaken, but it wasn't until weeks later that Jason realized how profoundly it had affected him. At first, Jason tried to suppress the emotions that lingered long after the accident. He wouldn't allow himself to feel or express anger, even when provoked by minor inconveniences on the job site. His coworkers began to notice a change in his demeanor - he was quieter, more withdrawn. Jason convinced himself that it was better this way; if he didn't acknowledge his feelings, they would eventually dissipate. But the memories persisted, and with them came an overwhelming sense of helplessness. Jason couldn't shake off the feeling that he'd been powerless to prevent the tragedy. He started to doubt his own competence on the job site, fearing that his mistakes might lead to another disaster. His anxiety led him to seek distractions, like late-night online gaming or impulsive trips to the casino. The rush of adrenaline was a fleeting escape from the crushing weight of his inadequacy. One evening, while working overtime, Jason caught himself zoning out on the job site, staring blankly into space as his coworkers bustled around him. It wasn't until one of them nudged him that he snapped back to reality. This deliberate dissociation had become a coping mechanism - a way to temporarily leave behind the turmoil brewing inside. Jason's shattered beliefs about the world were evident in his conversations with friends and family. He'd always thought of himself as someone who could control his environment, but now he felt vulnerable, like the universe was conspiring against him. His divorce from his wife had left emotional scars, and this new trauma had exposed them once more. As Jason struggled to make sense of his world, he found solace in solitary activities - fishing trips or long drives through the countryside. He'd try to recapture some semblance of control by meticulously planning each excursion, but even these small pleasures were tainted by his inability to shake off the memories. The tipping point came when a coworker was injured on the job site, and Jason's first instinct was to flee - not to help, but to escape the overwhelming sense of responsibility that came flooding back. That night, he realized he couldn't continue living like this. He made an appointment with a therapist, hoping to break free from the cycle of avoidance and self-doubt. As Jason sat in the waiting room, he knew it wouldn't be easy, but he was ready to confront the memories that had haunted him for so long. He hoped that by facing his fears head-on, he might reclaim some semblance of control over his life - and rediscover the man he once thought himself to be.
